newsitem.title: CHINA: China stock stamp duty hike cools share fever.
newsitem.headline: China stock stamp duty hike cools share fever.

text.p: China's recent hike in stamp duty on share purchases helped cool stock market fever by raising the cost of trading shares and cutting the money supply to the bourses, analysts said on Friday.
The tax, increased to 0.5 percent from 0.3 percent on May 10, had also become an important source of government revenue, the analysts said.

"The tax hike has greatly increased the cost of stock trading and helped cool down excessive speculation on the stock markets," said Xu Zhiling, deputy general manager of the trading department of China Guotai Securities.
"The tax acts like a funnel through which speculative funds are drained out of the stock markets," he said. "This has effectively cut hot (speculative) money supply to the markets."
Brokers estimated the tax hike had helped raise total transaction costs of stock trading on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges by about 34 percent.

The stamp duty had sucked about 75 million yuan ($9.0 million) a day from the country's two bourses in Shanghai and Shenzhen in the past three months, analysts said, with 30 million of that daily figure due to the May 10 increase.
The average combined daily turnover of the two exchanges is about 15 billion yuan ($1.81 billion).
"One key reason for the overheated trading earlier this year was a heavy oversupply of funds to the stock markets," a trader with a major Chinese securities house said.

China's stock prices surged around 50 percent from January to early May in a fever partly supported by euphoria surrounding the July 1 return to Chinese rule of the former British colony of Hong Kong.
The stamp duty increase was one of a series of measures Beijing took to cool that fever, including a ban on state banks, state enterprises and listed companies from trading stocks.
Share prices on the two bourses have fallen about 20 percent since the mid-year introduction of the measures.

"The tax hike, combined with the other crackdown measures, has exerted strong psychological pressure on investors because it shows that the central government is determined to curb overheated trading on the stock markets," one broker said.
China began to levy the stamp duty on stocks in Shenzhen in 1990 and in Shanghai in 1991. By June 1992, the tax was at a historical high of 0.6 percent.
In June 1992, Beijing ordered the tax cut to 0.3 percent -- where it stayed until May this year. China's tax law limits stock stamp duty to one percent.

As stock trading has becomes more popular, stamp duty income has surged, reaching more than 20 billion yuan in the first half of 1997, against 12.2 billion yuan for all of 1996, official figures show.
Analysts estimated income from the duty would reach around 40 billion yuan for all of 1997, equal to another major revenue source -- tobacco.
Finance Minister Liu Zhongli said in a recent speech that the increase in stock stamp tax contributed to China's budgetary surplus of 38.848 billion yuan in the first half of 1997.
Currently, 80 percent of China's stock stamp duty income goes to central government coffers and 20 percent goes to the local governments of Shanghai and Shenzhen.

Unlike many more developed countries, China did not levy personal income tax on stock trading, partly because its stock markets were still young and many aspects of the markets had not yet been regulated, analysts said.
